and vncommon entertainment, hee might keepe
Company with any Lord for his grace.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I, with any Lord that were past it.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
And such a good free hearted honest, affable kinde of

Gentleman: Come Boy a heauinesse will possesse me till I see
him.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose:
But youle finde your selfe heauyer then, by a seauen
hundred pound weight,—Alasse poore Birds that cannot
keepe the sweete Countrie, where they slye at pleasure, but
must needes come to London to haue their wings clipt, and
are faine to goe hopping home agen.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
So, No man is so impudent to denye that—
Spirits can change their shapes, and soonest of all into
Serjeants: because they are Coosen Germans to spirits, for
there's but two kinde of arrests till Doomes-day, the Deuill
for the soule, the Serjeant for the body, but afterward the deuill
arrests bodye and soule Serjeant & all, if they be knaues
still, and deserue it. now my yeoman ^aslight.

speeches.speaker: Fals.
prose: I Attend you good Serjant Shortyard.

speeches.speaker: Shor.
prose:
No more maister Blastfield now—poore Easie hardly
be set.

speeches.speaker: Fals^.
prose:
But how if he should goe to prison, weere in a madde
state then, being not Serjeants.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Neuer let^ come neere thy belee^e that heele take prison,
or stand out in lawe, knowing the debt to be due, but still
expect the presence of Maister Blastfield, kinde M. Blastfield,
worshipfull M Blastfield—and at the last—

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Maister Shortyard, maister Falslight.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: The Boy: a warning-piece,—see where he comes.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Is not in paules.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: He is not farre off sure sir.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: When was his hovre sayst thou?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Two sir.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Why two ha's strucke.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: No sir, they are now a striking.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Maister Richard Easie of Essex we arrest you.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Alasse a Surgeon, hee's hurt ith shoulder.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Deliuer your weapons quietly sir.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Why what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Y'are arrested at the suite of M. Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Maister Quomodo?

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
How strange you make it, you'r a landed Gentleman
sir, I knew tis but a trisse, a bond of seauen hundred pound.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
La, I knowe you had mistooke, you should arrest
One Maister Blastfield, tis his bond, his debt.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Is not your name there?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: True, for fashions sake.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Why and tis for fashions sake that we arrest you.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Nay, & it be no more, I yeelde to that: I know Maister
Blastfield wil see me take no iniurie as long as i'me in towne,
for Maister Alsups sake.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Whose that Sir?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: An honest Gentleman in Essex.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Oh, In Essex! I thought you had beene in London,
where now your busines lyes, honestye from Essex will be a
great while a comming sir, you should looke out an honest
paire of Cittizens.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Alasse sir, I knowe not where to finde e'm.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: No, there's enow in Towne.

speeches.speaker: Eas^.
prose:
I know not one by my troth, I am a meere stranger for
these partes, Maister Quomodo is all, and the honestest that
I knowe.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
To him then lets set forward:—Yeoman Spiderman,
castan eye about for Maister Blastfield.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Boy—Alasse the poore boy was frighted away at
first.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Can you blame him sir—we that dayly fray away
Knight's, may fright away Boyes I hope.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Ha? haue they him sayst thou?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: As sure as—

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: The land's mine, thats sure enough boy.
Let me aduaunce thee knaue, and giue thee a kisse,
My pl^t's so firme I dare it now to misse.
Now shall I be diuulgde a landed man,
Throughout the liuerie:—one points, another whispers,
A third frets inwardly: let him fret and hang,
Especially his enuie I shall haue,
That would be faine, yet cannot be a knaue,
Like an olde leather girt in furde Gowne,
Whose minde stands stiffe but his performance downe.
Now come my golden daies in:—whither is the worshipfull
master Quomodo, and his faire Bedfellow rid forth,
To his land in Essex? whence comes those goodly loade of
Logs? from his land in Essex? where growes this pleasant
fruit, sayes one Citizens wife in the rowe; at maister Quomodos
Orchard in Essex; oh, oh, do's it so, I thanke you for
that good newes yfaith.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Here they come with him sir.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Grant mee patience in my ioyes, that being so great
I run not mad with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Blesse maister Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
How now Serjeants? who ha you brought me here,
master Easie?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Why la you now Serjeants, did I not tell you you mistooke?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Did you not heare me say. I had rather ha had master
Blastfield, the more sufficient man a great deale?

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Verie true sir,—but this Gentleman lighting into
our hands first—

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Why did you so sir?

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Wee thought good to make vse of that oportunitie,
and hold him fast.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
You did well in that I must needes say, for your owne
securities, but twas not my minde master Easie to haue you
first, you must needes thinke so.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I dare sweare that master Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
But since you are come to me, I haue no reason to refuse
you, I should show little manners in that sir.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
But I hope you spake not in that sence sir, to impose

the bond vpon mee.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
By my troth that's my meaning sir, you shall finde
mee an honest man, you see I meane what I say, is not the
day past, the money vntendred, you'd ha me liue vprightly
maister Easie?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Why sir, you know maister Blastfield is the man.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Why sir, I know master Blastfield is the man, but is
he any more then one man? two entred into bond to mee, or
I'me fowly coozn'd.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: You know my entrance was but for fashion sake.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Why, ile a gree to you, you'l grant tis the fashion likewise
when the Bond's due to haue the money paid agen.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
So we told him sir, and that it lay in your worships
curtezie to arrest which you please.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Marie do's it sir, these fellowes know the law,—
beside, you offred yourself into Bond to me you know, when
I had no stomake to you, now beshrew your heart for your
labour, I might ha had a good substantiall Citizen, that
would ha paid the summe roundly, altho I think you sufficient
enough for seauen hundred pound, beside the forfeyture,
I would be loath to disgrace you so much before Serjeants.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
If you would hathe pacience sir, I doe not thinke but
master Blasefield is at Carriers to receiue the money.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
He wil proue the honester man then, & you the better
discharged, I wonder he should breake with me, t'was neuer
his practise, you must not bee angry with mee now, tho
you were somewhat hot when you entred into Bond, you
may easily go in angerly, but you cannot come out so.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: No, the Diuels in't for that.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Do you heere sir, a my troth we pittie you, ha you any
store of Crownes about you?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Faith a poore store, yet they shall be at their seruice
that will striue to doe me good,—we were both drunke last
night, and ^eer thought vpon the bond.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
I must tell you this, you haue fell in to the hands of a
most mercilesse deuourer, the verie gul athe citie, should you
offer him mony, Goods or lands now, hee'd rather haue your
bodie in prison, hee's a such a nature. Eas. Prison w'are vndon
then.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Hee's a such a nature, looke?—Let him owe any man
a spite^ what's his course: he will lend him mony to day, a
purpose to rest him tomorrow.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Defend me?

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Has at least sixteene at this instant proceeded in both
the Counters: some batchler, some masters, some doctors of
captiuitie of 20. years standing and he desires nothing more
then imprisonment.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Would Ma. Blastfield would come away.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
I, then things would not bee as they are—what
will you say to vs if wee procure you two substantiall subsidie
Cittizens to baile you spite on's heart, and set you at libertie
to finde out maister Blastfield.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Serjeant! here, take all, ile be deare to you, doe but
performe it.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Much.

speeches.speaker: Fals.
prose: Inough sweet Serjeant, I hope I vnderstand thee.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
I loue to preuent the malice of such a rascall, perhaps
you might find maister Blastfield to night.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Why, we lie together man, there's the iest on't.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Fie.—and youle seeke to secure your baile, because
they will be two Cittizens of good account, you must doe
that for your credit sake.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Ile be bound to saue them harmelesse.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: A pox on him, you cut his throte then,—no words.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: What's it you require me maister Quomodo?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
You know that before this time I hope sir, present
money, or present imprisonment.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: I told you so.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: We nere had money of you.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: You had commodities, an't please you

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Well, may I not craue so much libertie vpo~ my word,
to seeke out maister Blastfield?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Yes, and you would not laugh at me: wee are sometimes
Gulls to Gentlemen. I thanke 'em; but Gentlemen are
neuer Gulls to vs, I commend 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Vnder your leaue master Quomodo, the Gentleman
craues the furtherance of an houre, and it sorts well with our

occasion at this time, hauing a little vrgent busines at Guildhall,
at which minute weele returne, and see what agreement
is made.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Nay take him along with you Serjeant.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I'me vndone then.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Hee's your prisoner; and being safe in your house at
your owne disposing, you cannot denie him such a request:
beside, he hath a little faith in Ma. Blastfields comming sir.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Let me not be too long delaid I charge you.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Not an houre yfaith sir.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
O maister Easie, of all men liuing I neuer dream.
you would ha done me this iniurie: make me would my credite,
faile in my commodities, ring my state into suspition:
for the breaking of your day to me, has broken my day to
others.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
You tell me of that still, which is no fault of mine master
Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Oh whats a man but his honestie master Easie, and
thats a fault amongst most of vs all,—Marke but this note,
Ile giue you good counsell now,—as often as you giue
your name to a bond, you must think you christen a child, and
take the charge on't too: for as the one, the bigger it growes
the more cost it requires: so the other the longer it lies, the
more charges it puts you too, onely heer's the difference a
childe must bee broke, and a bond must not, the more you
breake children, the more you keep 'em vnder: but the more
you breake bondes, the more theyle leape in your face, and
therefore, to conclude, I would neuer vndertake to bee Gossip
to that bond which I would not see well brought vp.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Say you so sir?—Ile thinke vpon your counsaile
hereafter for't.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Ah foole, thou shouldest neere ha tasted such witte
but that I know tis too late.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: The more I grieue:

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: To put all this into the compasse of a litle hoop Ring
Make this account, come better dayes or worse,
So many bonds abroad, so many boyes at nurse.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
A good medicine for a short memorie:—but since,

you haue entred so farre, whose children are desperate depts
I pray?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: The desperate Debter hence deriues his name,
One that has neither money, land nor fame,
All that he makes, proue Bestards, and not Bonds,
But such as yours, at first are horn^ to lands.
prose:
Faith they are like the of-springs of stolne lust, put to
the hospital, their fathers are not to be found, they are either
too far abroad, or too close within, and thus for your memories
sake.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
But all that I beget heereafter ^le so one disinherit
Maister Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
In the meane time heeres a shrewd knaue will disinherit
you.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Well, to put you out of all doubt Maister Quomodo,
ile not trust to your curtezie, I ha sent for bayle.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: How? y'aue co^z^ed me there y^aith.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Since the worst comes to the worst, I haue those friends
'ith Cittie, I hope that will not suffer me to lye for seauen
hundred pound.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
And you tolde me you had no friendes heere at all,
how should a man trust you now?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: That was but to trie your Curtesie M. Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
How vnco~scionably he gulls himself—they must
be wealthye subsidie-men sir, at least fortye pound 'ith
Kings Bookes I can tell you, that doe such a feate for you.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Heere they come what so ere they are.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Berlady Aldermans Deputies, I am verie sorrye for
you sir, I cannot refuse such men.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Are you the Gentleman in distresse?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: None more then my selfe sir.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Hee speakes truer then he thinkes, for if he knew,
The hearts that owe those faces—a darke shop's good for
somewhat.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: That was all sir.

speeches.speaker: Shor.
prose:
And that's enough, for by that meanes' you
haue made your selfe ^able to the Bond, as well as that Basefield

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Blastfield sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Oh ^
^ou mercie tis Blastfield indeede.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
But vnder both your worships fauours I know where
to finde him presently.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: That's all your refuge.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Newes, good newes Master Easie.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: What boy?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose:
Maister Blastfield ^y maister ha^ receiued a tho ^
pound, and will be at his lodging at supper.

speeches.speaker: Easie.
prose:
Happy^ newes, heare you that Maister
Quomodo?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Tis enough for you to heare that, y'are the fortunate
man sir.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Not now I beseech your good worships.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Gentleman, what's your to^her name?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Easie.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
O Maister Easie—I would we could rather pleasure
you otherwise Maister Easie, you should soone perceiue
it, ile speake a proud word we haue pittied more Gentlemen
in distresse, then any two Cittizens within the freedome—
but to be baile to sea^en hundred pound action, is a matter
of shroud weight.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Ile be bound to secure you.

speeches.speaker: Shor.
prose: Tut, what's your bond sir?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Bodye, goods, and Lands, immediately before Master
Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Shall we venture once agen, that haue beene so often
vndone by Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Fal.
prose:
I haue no great stomacke too't, it will appeare in vs
more pittie then wisdome.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Why should you say so sir?

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
I like the Gentlemans face well, hee doe's not looke as
if he would deceiue vs.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: O not I sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Come weele make a desperate voyage once agen,

weele trye his honestie, and take his single bond, of body
Goods and Lands.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I dearely thanke you sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Maister Quomodo?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Your worships.

speeches.speaker: Shortyard.
prose:
We haue tooke a Course to set your prisoner
free.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Your worships are good baile you content me.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Come then, and be a witnesse to a Re^ullisance.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: With all my heart sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Maister Easie, you must haue an especiall care now
to find out that Blastfield.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I shall haue him at my lodging sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
The ^ will ^ you selse, Maister
Quomodo will come vpon vt, and ^ you.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I know that sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Well since I see you haue such a good minde to bee honest
^e lea^e some greater ^ sweate with you to
finde him my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
H^are then my mis^rie ends ^
A strangers kindenesse oft exceedes a friends.

verse: Thou art deceiu^d thy miserie but begins,
"To beguile goodnes, is the coare of sins.
My loue is such vnto ^hee, that I die

As often as thou drink'st vp ^
.
Yet haue no meanes to warne thee from't, for hee
"That sowes in Craft, doe's rape in Iealousie.

speeches.speaker: Rerrage.
prose:
Now the letters made vp and all, it wants but the
print of a s^ale, and away it goes to Maister Quomodo: Andrew
Le^he is well whipt in't, his name stands in a white
sheete heere, and do^s pennance for him.

speeches.speaker: Sale.
prose: You haue shame enough against him, if that be good.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose:
First as a contempt of that reuerend Ceremony, hee
has in hand, to wit, marriage.

speeches.speaker: Sale.
prose:
Why doe you say to wit marriage, when you knowe
theres none will marrie that's wise.

speeches.speaker: R^r.
prose:
Had it not more neede then, to haue wit to put too't if
it be growne to a ^olly?

speeches.speaker: Sale.
prose: Y'^ue ^un, ile giue't you.

speeches.speaker: Rerag.
prose:
Tis no thankes now,—but as I was saying: as a
soule contempt to that sacred ceremony, hee moste audaciouslye
keepes a Drab in towne, and to be free from the interruption
of blew Beadles, and other bawdy Officers, hee most
politickly lodges her in a Constables house.

speeches.speaker: Sale.
prose: That's a prettie point yfaith.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose:
And so the wa^ch that should fe^ch her out. are her
chiefest guard to keepeher in.

speeches.speaker: Sale.
prose:
It must needes be for looke how the Constable playes
his Conscience, the watch-men will followe the suite.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose: Why well then.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: All night from me hee's hurt, hee's made away.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Where shall we seeke him now? you leade me fayre
^aunt's sir.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Pray keepe a little patience sir, I shall finde him at last
you shall see.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
A Cittizen of my e^se and substance to walke so long
a foote.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
You should ha had my horse but that he ha's eaten out
his head sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: How would you had me hold him by the tayle sir then?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Manners forbid, tis no part of my meaning sir,—oh
heere's Maister Rerage, and Maister Salewood, now we shall
heare of him presently:—Gntlemen both.

speeches.speaker: Sale.
prose: Maister Easie, how fare you sir?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Verye well in health, did you see Maister Blastfield
this morning?

speeches.speaker: Sale.
prose: I was about to moue it to you.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose: We were all three in a minde then.

speeches.speaker: Sale.
prose: I ha not set eye on him these two daies.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose: I wonder he keepes so long from vs yfaith.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I began to be sicke.

speeches.speaker: Sal.
prose: Why, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Nothing in troth, but a great desire I had to haue
seene him.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose: I wo~der you shuld misse on't lately, you'r his bedfelow

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
I lay alone to night yfaith,—I doe not know how, O
here comes master Lethe, he can dispatch me: Master Lethe!

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose:
What's your name sir?—O crie you mercie master
Easie.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: When parted you from maister Blastfield sir?

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose:
Blastfield's an Asse, I haue sought him these two
dayes to beate him.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Your selfe all alone sir?

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose: I, and three more.—

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
I am glad, I am where I am then, I perceiue twas time
of all handes.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose: Content yfaith, let's trace him.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
What? haue you found him yet? neither? what's to be
done now? ile venter my bodie no further for any Gentlemans
pleasure, I know not how soone I may be cald vppon,
and now to ouer-heate my selfe.—

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Ime vndone.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
This is you that slept with him, you can make fooles
of vs, but ile turne you ouer to Quomodo fort.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Good sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Ile preuent mine owne danger.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I beseech you sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Tho I loue Gentlemen well, I doe not meane to bee
vndone for 'em.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Pray sir, let mee request you sir, sweete sir, I beseech
you sir.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Made fooles of vs! not to be found!

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: What, what?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Do not vndoe me quite tho Ma Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Y'are verie welcome, master Easie, I ha nothing to say
to you, ile not touch you, you may goe when you please,—
I haue good baile here I thanke their worships.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: What shall I say, or whom shall I beseech.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Gentlemen, S'lid they were borne to vndo vs I think,
but for my part, Ile make an oath before maister Qomodo
here, nere to doe Gentlemen good while I liue.

speeches.speaker: Fals.
prose: Ile not be long behind you.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Away; if you had any grace in you, you would bee ashamed
to looke vs ith face, ywis I wonder with what browe
you can come amongst vs, I should seeke my fortunes fa^re
enough if I were you, and neither returne to Essex, to bee a
shame to my predecessors, nor remaine about London, to be
a mocke to my successors.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Subtle Shortyard!

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Here are his lands forfeyted to vs master Quomodo,
and to auoyd the inconscionable trouble of law, all the assi^

^ance
he made to vs, we willingly resigne to you.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
What shall I doe with Rubbish, giue me money:
Tis for your worships to haue land, that keepe great houses,
I should be hoysted.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
But master Quomodo, if you would but conceyue it
aright, the land would fall fitter to you then to vs.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Curtzing about my land.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: You haue a towardly sonne and heyre as we heare.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: I must needs say, he is a Templer indeed.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
We haue neither posteritie in Towne nor hope for
any abroad; we haue wiues, but the markes haue beene out
of their mouths these twentie yeares, and as it appeares, they
did little good when they were in: wee could not stande about
it sir, to g^t riches and children too. tis more then one
man can doe. And I am of those Citizens mindes that say,
let our wi^es make shift for children and they will, they get
none of vs; and I cannot thinke, but he that has both much
wealth and many children, has had more helpes comming in
then himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
I am not a Bowe wide of your minde sir.—
And for the thristie and couetous hopes I haue in my sonne
and heyre Sim Qmomodo, that hee will neuer trust his land
in Waxe and Parchment as many Gentlemen haue done before
him.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Al y-blow for me.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
I will honestly discharge you, and recevue it in due
forme and order of law, to strengthen it for euer to my sonne
and h^yre, that he may vndoubtedly enter vppon't without
the let or molestation of any man, at his or our pleasure
whensoeuer.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Tis so assurde vnto you.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Why then maister Basie y'are a freeman sir, you may
deale in what you please, and goe whether you will. Why Tomazin,
maister Easie is dome from Essex, bid him welcome
in a cup of small Beare.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: Not onely vilde, but in it tyrannous.

speeches.speaker: Quom.
prose:
If it please you sir, you knowe the house, you
may visite vs often. and dine with vs once a quarter.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
verse: Confusion light on you, your wealth and heyre,
Worme gnaw your conscience, as the Moth your ware,
I am not the first heyre that rob'd, or beg'd.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Excellent excellent, sweet Spirits.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Landed maister Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: Delicate shortyard, commodious Falslight,
Hug and away, shift, shift.
Tis slight, not strength that giues the greatest lift.
Nowe my desires are full—for this tyme,
Men may haue Cormorant wishes, but alas
A little thing three hundred pound a yeare,
Suffices nature, keepes life and soule together,
Ile haue 'em l^pt immediately.
prose:
I long to warme my selfe by'th wood,—A fine iourney
in the Whitsun-holy dayes ^yfaith, to ride downe with
a number of Citizens, and their wiues, some vpon pillions,
some vpon S^de saddles, I, and little Tomazin ith middle our
some and heire S^m Quomodo in a peach colour Taffata Iack^t,
some hors^ length, or a long ^ard before vs, there will be
a fine shew on's I can tell you, where we Citizens will laugh,
and lie downe ge^ all our wiues with child against a bank and
get vp againe, ^stay, ha ^ast thou that wit yfaith twil. be admirable,
to see how the very thought of greene fieldes puts a
man into sweet inuenttions. I will presently possesse Sim

Quomodo of all the land, I haue a toy and ile doo't: and becau^e
I see before mine eies that most of our heires proue notorious
Rioters after our deaths, and that cousonage in the
father wheeles about to follie in the sonne, our posteritie
commonly foylde at the same weapon, at which we plaide
rarely. And being the world^ beaten worde, what's got ouer
the Diuels backe, (that's by knauerie) must be spent vnder
his bellie, (that's by lechery) being awake in these knowings,
why should not I oppose 'em now, and breake destinie
of her custome, preuenting that by pollicie, which without
it must needes be Destinie? and I haue tooke the course,
I will forthwith sicken, call for my keyes, make my Will,
and dispose of all, giue my sonne this blessing, that hee trust
no man, keepe his hand from a queane, and a Scriuener, liue
in his fathers faith, and doe good to no bodie: then will I begin
to raue like a fellow of a wide conscience, and for all the
worlde counterfeit to the life, that which I know I shall do
when I die, take on for my golde, my landes, and my wrytings,
grow worse and worse, call vpon the Diuell, and so
make an ende. by this time I haue indented with a couple of
searchers, who to vphold my deuice shall fray them out a'th
Chamber with report of sicknesse, and so la, I start vp, and
recouer agen: for in this businesse I will trust, no not my spirits
Falslight & shortyard, but in disguise note the condition
of al, how pittiful my wife takes my death, which wil appear
by Nouember in her eye, and the fall of the leaf inher bodie,
but especially by the cost she bestows vpo~ my funeral, there
shall I trie her loue and regard, my daughters marrying to
my will & lyking, and my sonnes affection after my disposing:
for to co~clude. I am as jealous of this land as of my wife,
to know what would become of it after my decease.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
prose: Tho I be poore, tis my glorie to liue honest.

speeches.speaker: Curt.
prose: I prethee doe not leaue me.

speeches.speaker: Faith.
verse: To be bawde.
Hell has not such an office,
I thought at first your minde had beene preseru'd,
In vertue and in modestie of bloud,

that such a face had not bene made to please the vnsetled Appetites
of seuerall men,
Those eyes turn'd vp through prayer, not through lust,
But you are wicked, and my thoughts vniust.

speeches.speaker: Curt.
prose:
Why thou art an vnreasonable fellow yfaith, doe
not al Trades liue by their ware, and yet cald honest Liuers?
doe they not thriue best, when they vtter moste, and make it
away by the great? is not hole-sale the chiefest marchandize?
doe you thinke some Merchants could keepe their wiues so
braue but for their hole-sale? you'r fowly deceiu'd and you
thinke so.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
prose:
You are so glewde to punishent and shame,
Your wordes ee'n deserue whipping—to beare the habit
of a Gentlewoman, and be in minde so distant.

speeches.speaker: Curt.
prose:
Why you foole you, are not Gentlewomen Sinners?
and there's no coragious Sinner amongst vs, but was a Gentlewoman
by the Mothers side I warrant you: besides, wee
are not alwaies bound to thinke those our fathers that marrie
our Mothers, but those that lye with our Mothers, and they
may be Gentlemen borne & born agen for ought we know,
you knowe.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
prose:
True: corruption may well be Generatious first,
Wee're bad by nature, but by custome worst.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: Oh my Husband.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: My Father, O my Father.

speeches.speaker: Fals.
prose: My sweete Maister, dead!

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Runne boy, bid 'em ring out, hee's dead, hee's g^ne.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Then is as arrant a knaue gone, as ere was cal'd vppon.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
verse: The happyest good that euer Shortyard felt,
I want to be exprest, my mirth is such,
To bee struck now eene when his ioyes were hye,
Men onely kisse their knaueries, and so dye,
Iu'e often markt it.
Hee was a famous Coozner while he liu'd,
And now his Sonne shall reape it, ile ha the lands,
Let him Studye law after, tis no labour
to vndoe him for euer: but for Easie,
Onely good confidence did make him foolish,
And not the lack of Sence, that was not it,
Tis worldly craft beates downe a Schollars wit,
For this our Sonne and heyre now, hee
From his conception was entayl'd an Asse,
And hee ha's kept it well, twentie fiue yeares now,
Then the sleightest art will doo't, the landes lye faire,
No Sinne to begger a deceiuers heyre.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Heere Wenefride, heere, heere, heere, I haue alwaies
found thee secret.

speeches.speaker: Wini.
prose: You shall alwaies finde me so Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: Take this letter and this Ring.

speeches.speaker: Wini.
prose: Yes forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Oh how all the partes about me shake,—enquire
for one Maister Easie at his olde lodging 'ith the Blackfryers,

speeches.speaker: Win.
prose: I will indeed forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Tell him the partie that sent him a hundred pound
tother day to co~fort his heart, ha's likewise sent him this Letter
and this Ring, which has that vertue to recouer him agen
for euer say—name no body Winifride.

speeches.speaker: Win.
prose: Not so much as you forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Good Girle, thou shalt haue a mourning Gowne at
the buryall of mine honestie.

speeches.speaker: Win.
prose: And ile effect your will a my Fedelitie.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
I doe account my selfe the happyest Widdowe that
euer counterfetted weeping, in that I haue the leasure now,
both to doe that Gentleman good, and doe my selfe a pleasure,
but I must seeme like a hanging Moonea little waterish
a while.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
verse: I entertaine both thee and thy Deuice,
Twill put e'm both to shame.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: That is my hope sir,
Especially that strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
verse: Saue you sweete widdowe,
I suffer for your heauinesse.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
O Maister Rerage, I haue lost the dearest husband
that euer woman did inioy.

speeches.speaker: Rerg.
prose: You must haue patience yet.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Oh talke not to mee of patience and you loue me,
good Maister Rerage.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose:
Yet if all tongues goe right, hee did not vse you so wel
as a man mought.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Nay, that's true indeed Maister Rerage, he nere vsd
me so well as a woman might haue beene vsde, that's certain
in troth ta's beene our greatest falling out sir, and though it
be the part of a widdowe, to show her selfe a woman for her
Husbands death, yet when I remember al his vnkindnesse,
I cannot weepe a stroake yfaith Maister Rerage, and therefore
wisely did a great widdow in this land, comfort vp
another, goe too Lady (quoth she) leaue blubbering, thou
thinkest vpon thy husbands good parts when thou sheddest
teares, doe but remember how often hee ha's laine from thee,
and how many naughtie slipperie turnes he has done thee, &
thou wilt nere weepe for him I warrant thee—you would
not thinke how that counsell ha's wrought with me Maister
Rerage, I could not dispend another teare now, and you
would giue me nere so much.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose:
Why I count you the wiser Widdowe, it showes you
haue wisdome, when you can checke your passion, for
mine owne part, I haue no sence to sorrowe for his death,
whose life was the onely Rub to my affection.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Troth and so it was to mine, but take courage now,
your'e a Landed Gentleman, & my Daughter is seauen hundred
pound strong to ioyne with you.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose: But Lethe lyes'ith way.

speeches.speaker: Tomaz.
prose:
Let him lye still,
You shall treade ore him or ile faile in will.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose: Sweete widdowe.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
What a beloude man did I liue? my Seruants gall their
fingers with ringing, my wiues cheeks smart with weeping,

stand in euerie corner, you may take water in my house—
but am not I a wise foole now? what if my wife should take
my death so to heart, that shee should sicken vppon't, nay
swone, nay dye? when did I heare of a woman doe so, let mee
see,—Now I remember me, I thinke twas before my
Time; yes, I haue heard of those wiues that haue wept, and
s^bd, and swound—marry I neuer heard but they recouered
agen, that's a co~fort la, that's a comfort, & I hope so will mine
—peace, tis nere vppon the time, I see, here comes the
worshipful liuerie, I haue the Hospital Boyes, I perceiue little
Tomazin will bestow cost of me,—Ile listen to the common
censure now, how the world tongues me when my ^are
lyes lowe.

speeches.speaker: 1. Liue.
prose:
Who Quomodo? meerely enricht by shifts,
And cousnages, beleeue it.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: I see the world is verye loath to praise me,
Tis Rawlye friendes with me, I cannot blame it,
For what I haue done, has beene to vexe and shame it.
Heere comes my Sonne, the hope, the landed heyre,
Ont whose rare thrift, will say mens tongues you lye,
Ile keepe by lawe what was got craftily.
Me thinkes I heare him say so:
He does salute the liuerie with good grace,
And solemne Gesture—

speeches.speaker: Bead.
prose:
oh my yong Worshipful M. you haue parted from
a deere Father, a wise and proui-dent father.

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose: Art thou growne an Asse now?

speeches.speaker: Bead.
prose: Such an honest Father—

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose:
Prethee Beadle leaue thy lying, I am scarce able to
endure thee yfaith, what honesty didst thou ere know by my
Father speake, rule your tongue Beadle least I make you
proue it, and then I knowe what will become of you, tis
the scuruy est thing i'th earth to belye the dead so, and hee's
a beastly Sonne and heyre that wil stand by, and heare his father
belyed to his face, hee will nere prosper I warrant him,
Troth if I be not asham'd to goe to Church with him, I would
I might be hang'd, I feare such filthye Tales goe on him, oh

if I had knowne hee had beene such a lewde fellow in his life
hee should nere haue kept me company.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Oh—o—o!

speeches.speaker: Sim.
prose:
But I am glad hee's gone, tho twere long first, Shortyard
and I will reuell it yfaith, I haue made him my Rentgatherer
alreadie.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Hee shall bee speedilye disinherited, hee gettes not a
foote, not the Crowne of a Mole-hill, ile sooner make a courtyer
my heyre for teaching my wife trickes then thee,
my moste neglectfull Sonne? Oh now the coarse, I shall obserue
yet farder.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
O my moste modest, vertuous and remembring wife,
she shall haue all when I dye, she shall haue all.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose:
Maister Easie? tis, oh what shift shall I make now?
oh—

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Sweete wife she sownes, ile let her alone, ile haue no
mercie at this time, ile not see her, ile follow the coarse.

speeches.speaker: Eas:
prose: The Deuill grinde thy Bones, thou co^sning Rascal.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose:
Giue her a little more ayre, tilt vp her head, comfort
thy selfe good widdowe, doe not fall like a Beast for a husband,
there's more then wee can well tell where to put e'm,
good soule.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: Oh, I shall be well anon.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose:
Fye, you haue no patience yfaith, I haue buried foure
Husbands, and neuer offered e'm such abuse.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: Couzen, how doe you?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Sorry to see you ill Couze.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: The worst is past I hope.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I hope so to.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: Lend me your hand sweet Couze I haue troubled you

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose:
No trouble indeed forsooth—Good Couzen haue
a care of her, comfort her vp as much as you can, and all little
ynough I warrant yee.

speeches.speaker: Tomaz.
prose: My moste sweete loue.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: My life is not so deere.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: I haue alwaies pittyed you.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Y'aue showne it heere.
And giuen the desperate hope?

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Delay not now, y'aue vnderstood my loue, I haue
a priest readye, this is the fittest season, no eye offends vs,
Let this kisse
Restore thee to more wealth, me to more blisse.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: The Angels haue prouided for me.

speeches.speaker: Short.
verse: I haue not Scope ynough within my brest,
To keepe my ioyes containde: I'me Quomodoes
heire: the Lands assurances, and all are mine
(I haue tript his Sonnes heeles vp) aboue the ground,
His father left him: had I not encouragement?
Do not I knowe what proues the Fathers pray?
The Sonne nere lookes on't, but it melts away.
Doe not I knowe the wealth that's got by fraude?
Slaue's share it like the ritches of a Bawde.
Why tis a curse vnquenchable, nere cooles.
Knaues still commit their consciences to fooles:
And they betray who o'wde em, heeres all the bonds,
All Easies writings, let me see:

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: Now my desires weare crownes.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
My ioyes exceede,
Man is neere healthfull, till his follyes bleede.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Oh, beholde the Villaine, who in all those shapes
Confounded your estate.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: That slaue, that villaine.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: So many Acres of good meadowe—

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Rascall.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: I heare you sir.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Rogue, Shortyard, Blastfield, Serjeant, Deputy, cousner

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Holde, holde.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I thirst the execution of his eares.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: Hate you that office,

speeches.speaker: Easi.
prose: Ile strip him bare for punishment and shame.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose:
Why doe but heare me sir, you will not thinke what I
haue done for you.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Giuen his Sonne my Lands.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
verse: Why looke you, tis not so, your not tolde true,
I haue Coosned him agen meerely for you,
Meerely for you sir, twas my meaning then
That you should wed her, and haue all agen.
prose:
A my troth 'its true sir: looke you then heere sir, you shall
not misse a little scrowle sir, pray sir, let not the Cittie knowe
me for a knaue, there be ritcher men would enuie my preferment
if I should be knowne before e'm.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
verse: Villaine, my hate to more reuenge is drawne,
When slaues are found, tis their base Arte to fawne,
Within there—.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: How now? fresh warders.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
This is the other, binde him fast, haue I found you
Maister Blastfield.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
verse: This is the fruite of Craft,
Like him that shootes vp hye, lookes for the shaft
And findes it in his fore-head, so does hit
The Arrowe of our fate, wit destroyes wit:
The head the bodyes bane, and his owne beares,
You hae Corne enough, you neede not reape mine eares,
Sweete Maister Blastfield.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I loath his voice, away.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: What happynesse was heere, but are you sure you haue all?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I hope so my sweete wife.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose:
What difference there is in Husbands, not onelye
in one thing, but in all.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
verse: These my good deedes shall to more safetie turne,
And these my bad haue their desarts and burne.
Ile see thee agen presently, reade there.
prose:
Heeres good deedes and bad deedes, the writings that
keep my lands to me, and the bonds that gaue it away from
me.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: Did he want all, who would not loue his care?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
What a wife hast thou Ephestian—Quomodo, so louing
so mindefull of her duetye not onely seene to weep but
knowne to swone, I knew a Widdow about Saint Antlings so
forgetfull of hir first Husband, that she marryed agen within
the tweluemonth, nay some berladye within the month:
there were sights to be seen, had they my wiues true sorrows
seauen nor seauen yeares would drawe e'm to the stake, I
would moste tradesmen had such a wife as I, they hope they
haue, wee must all hope the best: thus in her honour.

verse: A modest wife is such a Iewell,
Euerie Gold-smith cannot show it:
He that's honest, and not cruell,
Is the likelyest man to owe it.

prose:
And that's I, I made it by my selfe, and comming to her as a
Beadle for my reward this morning, ile see how shee takes
my death next her heart.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: Now Beadle.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Blesse your mistrisships eyes from too many teares,
Although you haue lost a wise and worshipfull Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: You come for your due Beadle, heere 'ith house.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Most certaine, the Hospitall money and mine owne
poore forty pence.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: I must craue a discharge from you Beadle.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Call your man, ile heartilye see my hand to a Memorandum.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose: You deale the truel yer.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Good wench still.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
George, heere is the Beadle come for his money, draw
a Memorandum that he has receiued all his due he can claim
heere ith house after this funerall.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
What politick directions shee giues him, all to secure
her selfe, tis time yfaith now to pitty her, ile discouer my selfe
to her ere I goe, but came it off with some liuely iest now, that
were admyrable: I haue it? after the memorandum is written
and all, ile set my owne name too't Ephestian Quomodo,

sheele start, sheele wonder how Ephest. Quomodo came the
ther that was buried yesterday: y'are beset little Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: Ninteene, twentie fiue pound, 1, 2, 3, & 4. d.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: So, we shall haue good sport, when tis read:

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: How now Ladie, paying away money so fast?

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: The Beadles due here sir

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Whose? tis Easie, what makes Easie in my house,
Hee is not my wiues ouer seer I hope:

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Whats here?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: He makes me sweate.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
Memorandum that I haue receiued of Richard Easie,
all my due I can claime here i'th house. or any hereafter for
me: In witnesse whereof, I haue set to mine owne hand,
Ephestian Qommodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: What haue I done? was I mad?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Ephestian Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
I, well, what then sir? get you out of my house,
First you maister Prodigall had land, away.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose:
What is the Beadle drunke or mad?
Where are my men to thrust him out a doores.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Not so good Tomazin not so.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: This fellow must be whipt.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Thanke you good wife.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I can no longer beare him.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: Nay sweete husband.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Husband I me vndone, beggard, couzend, confounded
for euer: married alreadie? will it please you knowe mee
now mistris Harlot, and master Horner, who am I now?

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: Oh, hee's as like my tother husband as can be.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Ile haue iudgement, ile bring you before a Iudge, you
shall feele wife whether my flesh be dead or no, ile tickle you
yfaith, yfaith.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: The Iudge that heele solicite knowes me well.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Lets on then, and our greeuances first tell.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose: Here they come.

speeches.speaker: Sus.
prose: O where.

speeches.speaker: Let.
verse: Hart of shame, vpo~ my wedding morning so disgracd.
Haue you so little conscience Officers,
You will not take a bribe?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose:
Master Lethe we may lie together lawfully hereafter,
for we are coupled together before people ynow yfaith.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
prose: There goes the strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Sus.
verse: Pardon my wilfull blindnesse and enioy me.
For now the difference appeares too plaine,
Betwixt a base slaue and a true Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
verse: I doe embrace thee in the best of loue,
How soone affections fail, how soone they proue.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: His cousnages are odious, he the plaintife,
Not onely framde deceitfull in his life,
But so to mocke his funerall.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
verse: Most iust.
The Liuerie all assembled, mourning weedes,
Throughout his house een down to his last serua~t
The Herauld richly hirde to lend him Armes,
Faind from his Auncestors, which I dare sweare knewe no
other Armes but those they labour'd with,
All preparations furnisht, nothing wanted
Saue that which was the cause of all, his death,
If he be liuing.

speeches.speaker: Iudg.
prose: Twas an impious part.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
verse: We are not certaine yet it is himselfe,
But some false spirit that assumes his shape,
And seekes still to deceiue mee.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Oh are you come? my Lord? their here, good morrow
Tomazin.

speeches.speaker: Iudg.
prose: Now what are you?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: I am Quomodo my Lord, & this my wife,
Those my two men, that are bound wrongfully.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
prose: How are we sure y'are he?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Oh you cannot misse my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
prose:
Ile trie you.
Are you the man that liu'd the famous cousner?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: O no my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Did you deceiue this Gentleman of his right,
And laid Nets ore his land?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Not I my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Then y'are not Quomodo but a counterfet,
Lay hands on him, and beare him to the whip.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Stay, stay a little I pray, now I remember me my Lord,
I cousned him indeed, tis wondrous true.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Then I dare sweare this is no counterfet.
Let all doubts cease this man is Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Why la you now, you would not beleeue this, I am
found what I am.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: But setting these thy odious shifts apart,
Why did that thought prophane, enter thy brest,
To mocke the world with thy supposed death?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Conceiue you not that my Lord? a policy.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
prose: So.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: For hauing gotten the lands I thirsted still,
To know what fate would follow 'em.

speeches.speaker: Iu^
prose: Being ill got.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Your Lorpship apprehends me.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
prose: I thinke I shall anon.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: And thereupon,
I out of policie possest my sonne,
Which since I haue found lewd, and now intend
To disinherit him for euer,
Not onely this was in my death set downe,
But thereby a firme triall of my wife,
Her constant sorrowes, her remembring vertues,

All which are Dewes, the shine of a next morning 'dries 'em
vp all I see't.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Did you professe wise cousenage, and would dare
To put a woman to her two dayes choice,
When of a minute do's it?

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: Lesse, a moment
The twinckling of an eye, a glimpse, scarce somthing do's it,
Your Lordship yet will graunt she is my wife.

speeches.speaker: Tom.
prose: O heauen!

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: After some penance, and the Deues of law
I must acknowledge that.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: I scarce like
Those Deues of lawe.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
verse: My Lord, altho the law too gently lot his wife,
The wealth he left behind he cannot chalenge.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Behold his hand against it.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
He do's deuize all meanes to make mee mad, that I
may no more lie with my wife in perfect memorie, I know't
b^t^et the landes will maintaine me in my wits: the lande
will doe so much for mee.

speeches.speaker: Iudg.
verse: In witnesse whereof I haue set to mine owne hand,
Eph^stian Quomodo.
Tis firme enough your owne sir.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: A iest my Lord, I did I knew not what.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: It should seeme so, deceit is her owne foe
Craftily gets, and childishly lets goe.
But yet the lands are his.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: I, warrant yee.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose:
No my good Lord, the lands know the right heire,
I am their master once more.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: Haue you the lands?

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: Yes truly I praise heauen.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Is this good dealing? are there such consciences abroad,
how? which way could he come by 'em?

speeches.speaker: Sho.
verse: My Lord ile quickly resolue you that it comes to me
This cousner whom too long I call'd my patrone,
To my thought dying, and the foole his sonne
Possest of all, which my braine partly sweat for,
I held it my best vertue, by a plot
To get from him what for him was ill got.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose: O beastly Shortyard!

speeches.speaker: Sho.
verse: When no sooner mine,
But I was glad more quickly to resigne.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
prose: Craft once discouer'd shewes her abiect line.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: He hits me euery where, for craft once knowne,
Do's teach fooles wit, leaues the deceiuer none.
My deedes haue cleft me, cleft me.

speeches.speaker: 1. Off.
prose: Roome there.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
verse: A little yet to raise my spirit.
Here maister Lethe comes to wed my Daughter.
That's all the ioy is left me: ha? who's this?

speeches.speaker: Iudge.
prose: What crimes haue those brought foorth?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: The shame of lust,
Most viciously on this his wedding morning,
This man was ceazde in shame with that bolde Strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Iudge.
prose: Why, tis she he meanes to matrye.

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose: No in truth.

speeches.speaker: Iudge.
verse: In truth you doe.
Who for his wife his Harlot doth preferre,
Good reason tis, that he should martie her.

speeches.speaker: Curt.
prose: I craue it on my knees, such was his vowe at first,

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Ile say so too
And worke out mine owne safetie,
Such was his vowe at first, indeede my Lord,
How ere his moode has chang'd him?

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose: O vilde slaue!

speeches.speaker: Curt.
prose: He sayes it true my Lord,

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Rest content,
He shall both marrie and taste punishment.

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose:
Oh intollerable!
I beseech your good Lordship if I must haue an outward punishment,
let me not marrie an inward, whose lastes will nere
out, but growe worse and worse: I haue a wife staies for
me this morning with seauen hundred pound in her pursse,
let me be speedily whipt and be gone, I beseech your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Hee speakes no truth my Lord, behold the Virgin,
Wife to a well esteemed Gentleman,
Loathing the Sin he followes.

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose: I was betrayed, yes faith.

speeches.speaker: Rer.
verse: His owne Mother my Lord,
Which hee confest through ignorance, and disdaine,
His name so chang'd to abuse the world and her.

speeches.speaker: Let.
prose:
Marry a Hailot, why not? tis an honest mans fortune,

I pray did not one of my Cou~triemen marrye my Sister? why
well then, if none should be marryed but those that are honest
where should a man seeke a wife after Christmas? I pitty that
Gentleman, that has nine Daughters to bestowe, and seauen
of e'm Seeded already, they wil be good stuffe by that time,
I doe beseech your Lordship to remoue the punishment, I
am content to marrie her.

speeches.speaker: Iudge.
prose: There's no remouing of your punishment.

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose: O good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Iudge.
verse: Vnlesse one heere assembled
Whom you haue most vnnaturally a busde, beget your pardon.

speeches.speaker: Leth.
verse: Who should that be?
Or who would doote, that has beene so abusde?
A troublesome pennance—sir.

speeches.speaker: Quo.
prose:
Knaue in your face, leaue your mocking, Andrew,
marrie your Qeane and be quiet.

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose: Maister Easie.

speeches.speaker: Eas.
prose: I'me sorrie you take such a bad course sir.

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose: Maister Quomodo.

speeches.speaker: Toma.
prose:
Enquire my right name agen next time, now goe
your waies like an Asse as you came.

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose:
Masse I forget my mother all this while,
Ile make her doo't at first, pray mother your blessing for
once.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Calst me Mother? out, I defie thee slaue.

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose:
Call me slaue as much as you will, but doe not shame
me now, let the world knowe you are my Mother.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose:
Let me not haue this Villaine put vpon me I beseech
your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Iudg.
verse: Hee's iustly curst, she loathes to know him now,
Whome he before did as much loath to knowe,
Wilt thou beleeue me woman?

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: That's soone done.

speeches.speaker: Iudge.
prose: Then knowe him for a Villaine, tis thy Sonne,

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Art thou Andrew my wicked Sonne Andrew?

speeches.speaker: Leth.
prose: You would not beleeue me Mother.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose:
How art thou chang'd?
Is this sute fit for thee? a Tooth-drawers Sonne,

this countrie has ee'ne spoilde thee since thou camst heather,
thy manners better then thy cloathes, but now whole cloathes
and ragged manners, it may well be saide that truth goes
naked, for when thou hadst scarce a shirt thou hadst more
truth about thee.

speeches.speaker: Iudg.
verse: Thou art thine owne affliction Quomodo:
Shortyard we banish, tis our pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Sho.
prose: Hence foorth no woman shall complaine for measure.

speeches.speaker: Iudg.
verse: And that all Error from our workes may stand,
We bannish Falslight euermore the land.
